content: A bezoar, also known as an enterolith, is a type of stone or concretion that forms in the gastrointestinal tract, primarily in ruminant animals but also in humans. These masses are composed of ingested foreign materials that accumulate and solidify within the digestive system. Bezoars are categorized based on their composition, with the most common types being trichobezoars, which are made of hair, and phytobezoars, which consist of indigestible plant material such as fruit or vegetable fibers. Typically, bezoars form in the stomach but can migrate into the small intestine, where they may cause obstruction. Factors that predispose individuals to bezoar formation include insufficient chewing of food, diets high in fiber, and a history of gastric surgery. Historically, bezoars were highly valued for their supposed medicinal properties, particularly as a universal antidote to poison. It was believed that a bezoar placed in a drinking vessel could neutralize any poison poured into it. The term bezoar is derived from the Persian word pâdzahr, meaning protection from poison. Interestingly, some trichobezoars have been shown to bind arsenic compounds, which were historically used as poisons. In 1575, the French surgeon Ambroise Paré conducted an experiment to test the efficacy of bezoars as antidotes. A cook, accused of theft, volunteered to ingest poison and attempt to cure himself with a bezoar. The experiment failed, and the cook died, disproving the belief that bezoars could counteract all poisons. This skepticism was echoed in a famous English legal case, Chandelor v. Lopus (1603), which established the principle of caveat emptor (let the buyer beware) when the effectiveness of a bezoar was called into question. The Merck Manual notes that certain foods, such as persimmons, have been linked to outbreaks of intestinal bezoars, with up to 90% of cases requiring surgical removal. In addition to their medical and historical significance, bezoars have been associated with sacred and mystical properties. In Hindu texts such as the Garuda Purana and Brihat-Samhita, bezoars are listed among the Nine Pearls, which include other rare and natural gemstones like the Conch Pearl and Cobra Pearl. These pearls were later documented in the 18th-century work Cabinet of Natural Curiosities by Albertus Seba, which featured detailed illustrations of bezoars and other rare artifacts. Some of these pearls, such as the Bamboo Pearl, form within plants, while others, like the Cloud Pearl, have no known formation process. Bezoars can take various forms depending on their composition. Food boli, which mimic true bezoars, are loose aggregates of food items such as seeds, fruit pits, or even substances like bubble gum and certain medications. Pharmacobezoars are composed of drugs, often forming semi-solid masses of tablets or liquid medications. Phytobezoars consist of indigestible plant material, such as cellulose, and are commonly seen in individuals with impaired digestion or reduced gastric motility. Trichobezoars, formed from ingested hair, are particularly notable in humans who compulsively consume hair, a condition sometimes referred to as Rapunzel syndrome. These hair-based bezoars often require surgical removal, and their presence can be confirmed through imaging studies such as fluoroscopy. Other less common types of bezoars include those formed from inorganic materials like stones or sand, which are more frequently observed in children. In traditional Chinese medicine, ox bezoars, known as Niu-huang, are used for their purported therapeutic properties. In alchemical practices, animal bezoars were created by pulverizing the heart and lungs of a viper, while mineral bezoars were derived from antimony and used as emetics or diaphoretics. Bezoars have also made appearances in popular culture. For example, a Darwin Award was given to an individual who died from a bezoar caused by compulsive hair-eating. Bezoars are mentioned in ancient Arabic and Persian texts, where they were classified as precious stones. A comprehensive monograph on bezoars was written in 1625 by Caspar Bauhin, a Swiss physician, summarizing the knowledge of bezoars at the time. In modern fiction, bezoars are famously referenced in the Harry Potter series, where they are described as stones from a goat's stomach that can protect against most poisons. Harry Potter uses a bezoar to save Ron Weasley’s life after he consumes poisoned mead.
